source: Besnard, Greathead, Baxter (2004) When mental models go wrong: co-occurrences in dynamic, critical systems
finding: Two events that happen as expected can be a coincidence, but the operator takes the first as the cause of the second and trusts the model more. Case: the Kegworth crash (Boeing 737-400, 8 Jan 1989). The crew shut down the healthy right engine. Vibration and smoke then dropped, which looked like proof of the choice. The faulty left engine was still vibrating and the crew did not look at it again.
numbers: 47 lives lost. Captain over 13,000 flight hours, first officer over 3,200, but only 76 hours on the 737-400 between them. Survey June 1989: 64% of airline pilots said the new digital engine display did not draw attention to rapid changes, 74% preferred the old one. Symptom relief lasted about 20 minutes.
quote: the understanding of the mechanisms generating the data is not a necessary condition
limits: One accident, re-analysed from the report. No experiment. The co-occurrence idea is argued, not tested. The authors say it differs from fixation (it concerns how the model is built, not how it persists).
agent_relevance: A pass that follows an action is not proof the action fixed the fault. The agent should not count a check as confirming a fix unless the check could have failed (G3). Relief of the symptom must not close the case.

source: Rankin, Woltjer, Field (2016) Sensemaking following surprise in the cockpit - a re-framing problem
finding: Interviews with airline pilots about surprise. Nine kinds of difficulty in re-framing were found. Two matter here: conflicting data (the crew first discards the warning and keeps the old frame, and only questions it when more odd behaviour appears) and getting stuck in a narrow reading (a crew finds support for its first hypothesis, then acts on it and stops looking for other causes).
numbers: 20 pilots (14 were instructors or examiners, mean 10,892 flight hours, mean age 49). Interviews 50 to 90 minutes. 48 cases of surprise coded, nine challenge categories.
quote: checklists and procedures encourage you to keep moving, not to understand the problem
limits: Retrospective interviews, so memory and self-presentation bias. The authors say no objective counts should be drawn. Mostly experienced western European pilots.
agent_relevance: Gives named activities (question, preserve, elaborate, compare, switch, seek frame) that can be written as program-checked moves. A checklist-like procedure can itself push the agent forward without understanding.

source: Rankin, Woltjer, Field (2016) - case 4, fuel imbalance (same paper)
finding: Case of garden-path fixation. A first officer saw a fuel imbalance warning, found a 600 kg difference between wing tanks, decided it was a fuel leak and ran the leak checklist. The captain came back and agreed. The checklist led to shutting down a healthy engine. The true cause was a damaged cross-feed valve. Because of the shutdown the crew never saw that one tank still held the pre-flight value. The first officer's early statement of the problem also blocked the captain's alternative frame.
numbers: One case. 600 kg imbalance.
limits: Single interview case, told from memory. The checklist reportedly had items to exclude other causes, so the failure was in using the checklist as confirmation, not in its design.
agent_relevance: Maps to our S5 revise and S6 impasse. The first explanation gets a checklist of confirming steps; the agent should instead run a step that could split the leak hypothesis from the valve hypothesis. A second agent that hears the first framing is primed by it (G4, G9).

source: Al Essa, Schmidt, Mamede, Knezevic, Zwaan, Magzoub (2026) Premature closure underlies bias in medical diagnosis in students: a randomised controlled experiment
finding: Salient distracting findings put early in a clinical case cut diagnostic accuracy and shortened reading time per word. Put at the end, they cut accuracy less and did not shorten time. This supports premature closure (decide early, stop processing) and not a conflict account (which predicts slower processing).
numbers: 58 of 105 fourth-year medical students took part, 12 vignettes, within-group incomplete block design. Mean accuracy: no distractor 0.269, distractor at start 0.110 (61% drop), distractor at end 0.168 (36% drop); F(2,693)=11.995, p<0.001. Distractor-linked errors: 0.129, 0.330, 0.302. Time effect F(2,636)=4.799, p<0.01 only for early distractor.
limits: Students, not experts. Instruction to work fast and use first impressions may have inflated the effect. Shorter time does not uniquely prove closure; confirmation bias could also fit. Single lab, UAE.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence matters, and early salient evidence shortens later processing. The scaffold can measure this directly: log tokens spent after the first hypothesis appears. A drop in later effort is a code-checkable fixation signal for G1.

source: Adams, Barth-Cohen (2024) Exploring student sensemaking when engaging with anomalous data
finding: Think-aloud interviews with students facing anomalies in lab data. Three steps: notice the anomaly, make an explanation of its cause, then decide to keep, remove, recollect or mitigate the data. The explanation they build drives the decision. The paper also reviews earlier work: students recall discarding anomalous data or redoing runs to get 'correct' data.
numbers: 6 students (Introductory Physics for Life Sciences lab, one university). Review cites Chinn and Brewer 1998 (dinosaur vignettes), Lin 2007 (chemistry lab reports), Johansen and Christensen 2020 (survey), Dunbar 1993 (goals to confirm or to explain shape use of conflicting data).
limits: Very small sample, qualitative, anomalies had technical causes only (not theory-challenging).
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: the stated cause of an anomaly decides the action, so the agent should state the cause as a testable claim before dropping or keeping a result (G2, G3).

source: Xie, Zhang, Chen, Lou, Su (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: revealing the behavior of LLMs in knowledge conflicts (ICLR 2024)
finding: LLMs accept coherent counter-evidence that is the only evidence given. But when evidence supporting their own stored answer is also present, they favour it over the conflicting evidence: a strong confirmation bias. Bias is stronger for popular facts, grows with the number of own-belief evidence pieces at fixed ratio, and depends on evidence order for some models. Crude counter-evidence made by swapping an entity is mostly ignored, larger models more so.
numbers: GPT-4 memorization ratio about 80% on the most popular questions. Order effects: ChatGPT favours first-shown evidence; PaLM2 and Llama2-7B favour later evidence, with swings above 30% for those two. Models tested include ChatGPT-0301, GPT-4-0314, PaLM2, Llama2-7B/70B, Vicuna-7B/33B, Qwen-7B.
quote: LLMs also demonstrate a strong confirmation bias when the external evidence contains some information that is consistent with their parametric memory
limits: Factual QA (POPQA and similar), old model versions, counter-evidence written by another LLM. Not diagnosis or multi-step tasks.
agent_relevance: Mixing prior-consistent text into the context lowers the weight of the anomaly. The agent should show the anomaly alone, in a fresh context, without the current frame (S1/S2), and should randomise evidence order in code (G4, G5).

source: Wu, Wu, Zou (2024) ClashEval: quantifying the tug-of-war between an LLM's internal prior and external evidence (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks)
finding: Models adopt wrong retrieved content and overwrite their own correct answer. The more the content deviates from truth the less it is adopted. The less confident the model is in its first answer (token probability), the more it follows the context. A simple rule using token probabilities improves accuracy.
numbers: >1200 questions, 6 domains, 6 LLMs. Wrong context overrides correct prior over 60% of the time. Best model Claude Opus: accuracy 74.3%, context bias 15.7%, prior bias 2.1%. Each 10% rise in the prior's probability lowers the chance of following context by 4.5%. Calibrated token-probability correction: accuracy +14%, context bias -20%, prior bias 2% to 8.5%; random replacement at the same 8.5% bias gives 57.5% vs 75.4% for the method.
quote: overriding their own correct prior knowledge over 60% of the time
limits: Single-answer factual questions with injected numeric perturbations; the 'anomaly' is a planted document error, not a natural surprise. Needs token probabilities.
agent_relevance: Shows both failure modes: over-trusting new evidence and over-trusting the prior. Argues for a code-side comparison of with-evidence and without-evidence answers and their confidence, not a model decision (G5).

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gains from self-correction in earlier papers come from using the correct answer to decide when to stop. With no outside signal, accuracy stays flat or falls. The model cannot tell when its reasoning is wrong, so it changes right answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CSQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0. Intrinsic, after 2 rounds: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 74.7, CSQA 41.8 (from 75.8), HotpotQA 25.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 89.0 (from 95.5), CSQA 80.0, HotpotQA 43.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction
limits: Only GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2; one prompt style per source paper; HotpotQA sample small (100).
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2 and G1: revise only from a real failing output, and do not ask the model 'review your answer' on a schedule.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: When information arrives piece by piece, models guess early, produce a full answer early and then lean on that answer. When new facts contradict it, they often do not recover. Most of the loss is unreliability, not lost aptitude.
numbers: Average performance drop of 39% from single-turn to multi-turn across six generation tasks, over 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude fell about 15% and unreliability rose about 112% (figure label).
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Simulated users (a low-cost LLM reveals 'shards' of instructions). Tasks are underspecification, not anomalies in a model of the world. Numbers are averages over many models.
agent_relevance: An early full answer acts like an initial frame. The scaffold should keep early attempts as drafts and restart from a clean restatement plus all facts when new evidence comes in (S1 re-entry), instead of patching the old text.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (ICLR 2024)
finding: Five AI assistants wrongly admit mistakes when questioned, give feedback biased toward the user's stated view, and copy user errors. Human and preference-model raters sometimes prefer a convincing sycophantic answer to a correct one. This is the opposite fixation failure: dropping a right frame under pushback.
numbers: Five assistants, four free-form tasks. Exact rates not extracted (only the abstract and introduction were read).
limits: Only abstract and introduction read this session. Training-based explanation (RLHF preference data) is argued, not proven causal.
agent_relevance: Challenge text can flip a correct answer. A challenge should be turned into a test the code can run, not a message the model gives in to (G2, G5).

source: Mickelberg, Walker, Ecker et al. (2025) Did he or didn't he? Mixed evidence for the continued influence of retracted misinformation on person impressions
finding: A retracted negative fact about a person (for example a man who kicked his dog) kept influencing impressions in one of three experiments and was fully discounted in the other two. The paper says retracted event-related misinformation does show continued influence, but person impressions do not do so consistently. A proposed moderator is whether the false item fits a coherent causal story.
numbers: Three experiments, one internal random-effects meta-analysis (summary effect figures not extracted). Intro cites two meta-analyses of misinformation correction (Chan et al. 2017; Walter and Tukachinsky 2020) and Anderson, Lepper, Ross 1980 on explanation and persistence.
limits: Online impression tasks, not diagnosis. Sample sizes not extracted. Shows the effect is a boundary-conditioned one, not universal.
agent_relevance: A retracted claim stays in context and can keep pulling. Remove a refuted hypothesis from the working state in code (not just 'ignore it') and keep a list of ruled-out causes outside the prompt.

source: Croskerry, Singhal, Mamede (2013) Cognitive debiasing 1: origins of bias and theory of debiasing
finding: Narrative review of bias origins and debiasing. Offers a general checklist whose items map to anomaly handling, for example 'Did I just accept the first diagnosis that came to mind?' and 'Did I consider other organ systems besides the obvious one?' Notes that analytic (system 2) reasoning is also error-prone.
numbers: No effect sizes in the part read. Review only.
limits: Narrative review, skimmed for structure, not a systematic read. Checklists are cited as a proposal; effect on error is not shown here.
agent_relevance: Questions like these are prompts to the model, which G1 forbids on a schedule. Keep them only as responses to a failed check.

source: Chinn, Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition: a theoretical framework and implications for science instruction. Review of Educational Research 63(1), 1-49
finding: Proposes that a person with a theory can respond to contradicting data in a small set of ways: ignore it, reject it (doubt the data), declare it uncertain, exclude it (say it is out of the theory's scope), hold it in abeyance (wait for a future theory), reinterpret it (keep the theory, explain data as fitting), make a peripheral change to the theory, or change the theory. Only the last is full belief change. Factors named: prior belief entrenchment, ontological and epistemological commitments, background knowledge, and the quality of the anomalous data and any alternative theory. (Recalled from memory; PDF returned HTTP 403 in this session.)
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Full text blocked (university repository 403). Taxonomy built from psychology, history and philosophy of science, not from a single experiment.
agent_relevance: Gives a closed list of eight responses that the program could label from the transcript. A log of runs coded by these labels would show which cheap responses (ignore, reject, reinterpret) our agent uses most.

source: Chinn, Brewer (1998) An empirical test of a taxonomy of responses to anomalous data in science. J. Research in Science Teaching 35(6), 623-654
finding: Empirical test of the 1993 taxonomy with students given anomalous data on a theory (dinosaur vignettes per the description in Adams and Barth-Cohen 2024). Said to find that students used the whole range of responses and that most did not make full theory change. Details recalled only in outline.
numbers: Not verified: sample sizes and per-response percentages were not read.
limits: Not opened (paywalled). Only the vignette topic is confirmed, through a secondary source that I read (a05). Vignette reasoning, not live inquiry.
agent_relevance: The test design (give a theory, then data against it, then ask what the reader thinks) can be copied as a probe of our agent: an anomaly-injection test with coded responses.

source: Chinn, Brewer (2001) Models of data: a theory of how people evaluate data. Cognition and Instruction 19(3); and Responses to anomalous data on controversial topics and theory change. Learning and Instruction 11 (2001)
finding: Follow-up work on the same framework for controversial topics. Only the title and year were seen in a catalogue listing (cited 75 times); nothing of the findings was read.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened. Listed for forward-citation tracking only. The first title is from memory and may be incomplete.
agent_relevance: Pointer for the angle B/C agents to check the effect of topic strength on response.

source: Lord, Ross, Lepper (1979) Biased assimilation and attitude polarization: the effects of prior theories on subsequently considered evidence. J. Personality and Social Psychology 37
finding: Classic result. People with opposing views on capital punishment read the same mixed evidence. Each side rated the study that fit its view as better done and became more extreme. Recalled from memory: about 48 undergraduates, two studies and critiques.
numbers: Not verified this session (N about 48 recalled).
limits: Not opened. Later work disputes irrational reading: Jern, Chang, Kemp 2014 'Belief polarization is not always irrational' and Cook and Lewandowsky 2016 show Bayesian models can reproduce polarization (seen as catalogue titles only). Also a review in 1993 on the 'attitude polarization phenomenon' (title only).
agent_relevance: The evidence-quality rating itself is biased by the frame. Never let the frame-holder rate the anomalous source (G5, G8).

source: Anderson, Lepper, Ross (1980) Perseverance of social theories: the role of explanation in the persistence of discredited information. J. Personality and Social Psychology 39, 1037-1049
finding: Cited in a11 (reference list read; the result was not). Known result from memory: when people write an explanation of why a (later discredited) link holds, the belief outlasts debriefing more than when they do not. Explaining builds causal support that survives retraction of the data.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened. Only the citation and title were seen in a11.
agent_relevance: Asking the model to explain a hypothesis before testing it may entrench it. This predicts that a 'justify your answer' step before a check can harm later revision; the agent should test first and explain after.

source: Wason (1960) On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task. Quarterly J. Experimental Psychology 12, 129-140
finding: The 2-4-6 task. People announce rules that fit 2-4-6 and test with instances that fit their rule. Many never test a case that would break it. Recalled: only a minority gave the right rule on the first announcement.
numbers: Not verified (about 29 subjects recalled).
limits: Not opened. Later work (Klayman and Ha 1987) argues the positive test strategy is often sensible, so the 'failure' is partly about which tests are informative. Besnard et al. 2004 (a01) cites Klayman and Ha for confirmation bias.
agent_relevance: Our own check design must contain a test that the current rule predicts will fail (G3). Fitting examples is the same as the 2-4-6 positive test.

source: De Keyser, Woods (1990) Fixation errors: failures to revise situation assessment in dynamic and risky systems
finding: Defines a fixation error as keeping an erroneous situation assessment after cues to revise it. Forms: the This and That type (stuck on one explanation) and the Everything is Fine type; also a third form where several explanations are tried in turn. Recalled from memory. Both a01 and a02 cite it for the term.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened. Definition seen only through citations in a01 and a02. The Delft report 'Is overcoming of fixation possible' (2002) and an Anaesthesia editorial (2009) were found by search but could not be downloaded.
agent_relevance: Gives a time-based definition the code can use: the same hypothesis is kept after N cues or checks that disagree with it.

source: Klein, Phillips, Rall, Peluso (2007) A data-frame theory of sensemaking. In Hoffman (ed.), Expertise out of context
finding: Sensemaking is a cycle between data and frame. A frame holds the data; data reshape the frame. Activities: seeking and connecting data, elaborating, questioning, preserving, comparing, re-framing, seeking a frame. Preserving includes explaining anomalies away. Rankin et al. (a02) report that once a plausible frame is found the search for other causes stops (citing this work), and describe the same activities in their cases.
numbers: Not verified. The book chapter's own case counts were not read.
limits: Not opened; known through Rankin et al. 2016 only. A direct read is the job of the parallel data-frame agent.
agent_relevance: The frame can be stored as a plain rule plus a list of anomalies seen. A threshold on that list (not model judgement) can trigger question-frame.

source: Feltovich, Coulson, Spiro (2001) Learners' (mis)understanding of important and difficult concepts; Feltovich, Hoffman, Woods, Roesler (2004) Keeping it too simple: how the reductive tendency affects cognitive engineering. IEEE Intelligent Systems 19(3)
finding: Knowledge shields: reasoners protect a simple, partly wrong model by explaining away or discounting what does not fit, using a stock of ready moves. The reductive tendency holds that oversimplified explanations are kept because they work often enough. Rankin et al. cite Feltovich and Hoffman 2004 for stuck-in-a-frame despite contradicting data (a02).
numbers: Not verified. A search for the 2001 text found no open copy.
limits: Not opened. Shield list not read, so none are quoted. The 2001 paper title above is from memory.
agent_relevance: Gives a candidate list of explaining-away moves that could be detected as phrases in the model's reasoning, but G10 says text is weak evidence; use check outcomes instead.

source: Thagard (1989) Explanatory coherence. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 12(3), 435-467 (ECHO model)
finding: A connectionist network (ECHO) where hypotheses and evidence are nodes, explanation links are excitatory and contradictions inhibitory. Activation settles into an accepted set. Principles include symmetry, simplicity, analogy, and data priority (data get some automatic support). Used to model scientific revolutions and jury judgement. A theory with many explanatory links resists a single anomaly; a rival that explains the anomaly can win.
numbers: Not verified. Only catalogue hits (for example a 2023 Ising-model version of explanatory coherence, and a 1992 adversarial ECHO paper) were seen.
limits: Not opened. Recalled from memory. Critics note that weights are set by hand.
agent_relevance: A tiny version is codeable: a graph of hypotheses and evidence, with a count of unexplained data per hypothesis. The unexplained count is a program-side anomaly signal (G5).

source: Kulkarni, Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation. Cognitive Science 12 (KEKADA model)
finding: KEKADA is a production-system model of Krebs's urea-cycle discovery. A surprising result triggers a focus on it: it looks for the cause by changing the experiment and tracks the surprise until it is explained. Surprise is defined as a violated expectation set by the program. Recalled from memory; only a 1990 follow-up title ('Experimentation in machine discovery') was seen.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened. Model of one case history, not tested against many people.
agent_relevance: Offers a formal trigger: a mismatch between a stored prediction and an observed value starts a sub-goal. This matches the S6 impasse design and gives surprise a number.

source: Dunbar (1993) Concept discovery in a scientific domain. Cognitive Science 17; Dunbar (1997) How scientists think: on-line creativity and conceptual change in science
finding: Students solved a genetics-control task. Those given the goal of finding an explanation for unexpected results discovered the mechanism more often than those told only to test a hypothesis (outcome direction recalled; Adams and Barth-Cohen 2024, a05, summarise the 1993 result as: goals to confirm or to explain shape how conflicting data are used). In-vivo studies of molecular biology labs found unexpected results to be common and mainly handled by checking methods first, then by seeking a pattern across several anomalies.
numbers: Not verified. Exact discovery rates and the share of unexpected findings were not read.
limits: Not opened. Lab-meeting analysis is observational. Trickett et al. 2009 (How do scientists respond to anomalies?) was found but the PDF returned HTTP 403.
agent_relevance: The goal given to the model changes how it treats an anomaly. A slot instruction 'explain this mismatch' differs from 'confirm the rule', and the program should choose the first after a failed check (G1).

source: Gershman (2019) How to never be wrong. Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 26
finding: Bayesian account of why holding on to a theory can be rational: when data conflict, the blame can fall on an auxiliary hypothesis (instrument, assumption) instead of the main theory. Explaining away an anomaly through an auxiliary is then a probabilistic update, not a plain bias. Only the title was found in a catalogue search; the abstract summary is from memory.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened. Recalled summary; a formal account that can excuse any amount of explaining away unless priors on auxiliaries are constrained.
agent_relevance: Our agent needs a price for each auxiliary excuse: every 'maybe the test is broken' must be paid for with a check of the test (G3). Otherwise anomaly handling has no limit.

source: Klayman, Ha (1987) Confirmation, disconfirmation, and information in hypothesis testing. Psychological Review 94, 211-228
finding: Argues that the positive test strategy (test cases the hypothesis says are positive) is not the same as confirmation bias and is often a good heuristic, but it fails when the hypothesis is too broad or too narrow relative to the truth. Seen only as a citation in a01.
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Not opened. Competing explanation to Wason's reading of 'failure to disconfirm'.
agent_relevance: The cure is not 'always seek disconfirmation' but test a case where the rule and the main rival make different predictions.

source: Rudolph and colleagues on diagnostic problem solving and garden-path fixation in simulated anesthesia crises (Rudolph 2003 thesis; Rudolph and Raemer 2004, Anesthesia and Analgesia 98 S34)
finding: Anesthesia residents in simulated crises were found to fall into fixation on a first diagnosis (the garden-path pattern), with some residents still fixed after many cues. Recalled from memory; the WebSearch quota ran out before a source could be found, and no open copy was reached.
numbers: Not verified: sample size and fixation rate unknown.
limits: Not opened, and the citation details are from memory and may be wrong. Treat as a pointer only.
agent_relevance: Needs verification before use. If confirmed, simulator work would give a base rate of fixation for expert-like participants, useful for our test designs.

source: Cross-source note: two unrelated results both show stored frame beats new evidence at the point of decision (a06, a07, a09, a11) versus dropping a right frame under pushback (a10)
finding: LLM evidence is two-sided. Models over-weight their prior when prior-consistent text is present (a06), or over-weight wrong context (a07: more than 60% override). They also stick with early guesses in long exchanges (a09) and cave to challenge (a10). The same model can do either, so a fixed rule such as 'trust the new evidence' or 'trust the first answer' will not work.
numbers: Combined from a06 (GPT-4 about 80% memorization on popular questions), a07 (over 60% override), a09 (39% drop), a08 (GPT-3.5 CSQA 75.8 to 41.8 on self-correction).
limits: Different tasks, models and years. This is my synthesis from the opened papers, not a finding in any one of them.
agent_relevance: The trigger and the response must both come from code: compare outputs of independent runs or checks, then choose by a rule. No single default direction is safe.

source: Cross-source note: what the opened sources do and do not show about triggers for reframing
finding: Opened sources give three computable trigger signals. (1) A new cue arrives that the current frame did not predict (a02: crew questioned the frame only after other odd behaviour appeared). (2) Reduced effort after an early hypothesis (a04: time per word falls, accuracy drops). (3) A check on a held-out case fails (a08: gains only when a true signal exists). None of the opened sources timed a tolerance threshold or compared a count-based rule to judgement; that gap is still open.
numbers: No threshold data in any opened source.
limits: Own synthesis. The question in SUBFIELDS.md (do experts tolerate a count of anomalies before reframing?) is not answered by any source I could open; Dunbar and Trickett were the likely sources and were blocked.
agent_relevance: Use trigger 1 and 3 as G1 signals. Trigger 2 can be logged as a detector of fixation. A threshold must be set from our own logs and marked [O] or [D], not [E].

source: Access note for follow-up agents
finding: Blocked or unreachable in this session: Illinois IDEALS PDF of Chinn and Brewer 1993 (HTTP 403), Wiley PDFs (Trickett 2009 and an Anaesthesia editorial on fixation, 403), TU Delft fixation report (connection refused), Middlesex eprint on frames (connection refused), escholarship PDFs (empty). WebSearch quota was used up by others and OpenAlex free budget ran out mid-run. Europe PMC and arXiv were reachable.
limits: Applies to this run only.
agent_relevance: Angle B/C agents should try the same primary papers when quotas refill, or ask the user to supply the Chinn and Brewer 1993 and 1998 PDFs.
